entities.summary:
Charles de Valois, Duke of Angoulême (1573–1650), an illegitimate son of King Charles IX of France and Marie Touchet, navigated the turbulent political landscape of late Valois and early Bourbon France. Born in Barraux, Dauphiné, his lineage placed him at the heart of court intrigue, even without direct succession rights. He was recognized by his father and later ennobled, becoming Count of Auvergne and Duke of Angoulême. His life spanned a critical period of French history, marked by religious wars, consolidation of royal power under Henry IV, and the foundational years of Cardinal Richelieu’s ascendancy, positioning him as a minor but persistent figure in the machinations of the French aristocracy.

His career was characterized by both military service and a propensity for political miscalculation. Early in his life, he was implicated in the conspiracy of Marshal Biron against King Henry IV in 1604, leading to his imprisonment in the Bastille for eleven years, a significant disruption to his ambitions. Upon his release in 1616, he largely rehabilitated himself through loyal service, participating notably in the sieges of La Rochelle (1627–1628) and Montauban, and engaging in diplomatic missions to the Holy Roman Empire and England. His military contributions under Louis XIII and Richelieu helped to reinforce royal authority against Protestant strongholds and foreign adversaries, demonstrating his pragmatic adaptation to changing political tides.
